lessons.title: يوم (yawm) — "day," a word shared across the whole Semitic family
lessons.gloss: "day" — a true pan-Semitic word, cognate with Hebrew yom (as in Yom Kippur)

segments.text: This word is bigger than Arabic — it's one of the oldest, most widely shared words across the entire Semitic language family.

يوم (yawm) — "day" — root y-w-m. Arabic's day-names can compound with yawm — يوم الجمعة (yawm al-jumʿa, "day of the gathering") is the full, formal way to say "Friday," the exact same "day-of-X" construct-state pattern as Latin's diēs Lūnae — but colloquially, the bare day-name alone (al-jumʿa, as-sabt, already taught earlier) is just as common. Yawm itself is also the ordinary, standalone word for "a day."

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — A true Common Semitic word

segments.text: Yawm traces to Proto-Semitic yawm- — and this isn't just an Arabic word with foreign relatives, it's a genuinely Common Semitic word, found with the same shape and meaning across the whole family: Hebrew יוֹם (yōm — yes, the yom in Yom Kippur, "Day of Atonement"), Akkadian ūmum, and Aramaic yawmā. Four different Semitic languages, one shared ancient word for "day."

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — Beyond Semitic, honestly flagged

segments.text: Links beyond the Semitic family have been proposed, but none is established. A suggested tie to an Egyptian word for "sun" does not hold up: Egyptian's ordinary word for "day", ḥrw, is unrelated. The Semitic cognates above are the solid part of this word's story.

segments.text: What Hebrew word, familiar from a well-known holiday name, is yawm's direct cognate? (Yōm, as in Yom Kippur.) Name two other Semitic languages that share this exact word for "day." (Akkadian ūmum, Aramaic yawmā.) Is any link beyond the Semitic family established? (No — the Semitic cognates are the solid part.)
